title: Ahead, or Better Off
scopeNote: This keeps the allocation task performed and the full four-option structure, cut from six allocations to four, and keeps the three starting positions, which are the original tool's own addition and carry the critical content. The sorting task and the exercise in judging published claims are in the longer version.
summary: Four allocations between two anonymous strangers when you cannot allocate to yourself. The option that puts your category furthest ahead gives it fewer points than the option that gives it most, on all four.
learningObjectives: Explain why choosing maximum difference rather than maximum ingroup profit is the finding that matters.
Explain why a self-interest account cannot reach it.
Say what an allocation pattern cannot establish about why people chose as they did.
Recognise that the same allocation creates an inequality from one starting position and widens one from another.
State what the minimal group design removes on purpose, and what follows for generalising from it.
interactionTypes: a prediction about what most people do
four allocations the learner actually makes
every option written out in full with its point values
a live count of what each choice cost the learner's own category
the same choices scored against three different starting positions
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. Nothing is measured about the reader and there is no score.
dataStatus: Invented categories with no content, and invented allocation matrices. Nothing here reproduces the matrices, procedure or data of any published study.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout. Every option is written out in full with both point values in its label, so no allocation has to be read from a grid or a figure. Once an allocation is made its options are locked with aria-disabled rather than the disabled attribute, so they stay reachable and readable, and each explains in words what kind of option it was and, for the maximum-difference option, exactly what it cost. The three starting positions are compared in a real table with row and column headers whose final column is a sentence. Nothing is timed and there is no motion.
simulationNotes: Each allocation offers four options: an even split, the largest total, the most the set can give the learner's own category, and the largest lead for it. The last always gives the learner's category fewer points than the third, which is the whole paradigm, and the test suite verifies on every allocation that each option really is the maximum of its kind and that the largest-lead option costs the learner's category between five and seven points. Choosing it on all four costs Kestrels 23 points while raising their total lead from 11 to 45. The largest-total option always favours the other category slightly, so it cannot be confused with favouritism. Option order is rotated per allocation so the maximum-difference option is not in the same position every time and cannot be found by habit; the test suite checks that it moves. The three starting positions are scored from identical allocations, and the table reports the gap before and after so that the same act reads as creating an inequality, widening one or narrowing one depending only on where the categories stood. A learner who never chooses the largest lead is told their result is perfectly ordinary rather than corrected.
readmeTopic: why people pay points to be further ahead when they cannot benefit at all
